statement: The error signal $e$ is the positive or negative difference between the actual value $y$ (as measured at the output) and the wanted value $r$ (the control input) of a measurable variable in a closed-loop control system: $e = y - r$ (or $e = r - y$).

symbols.meaning: error signal, the difference between actual and wanted values
actual value of the system output as measured by a transducer

properties.property: The error signal is amplified and used via negative feedback to drive the motor/actuator in the direction necessary to reduce or eliminate the error toward zero.
properties.why: Closed-loop control uses error-sensing negative feedback to correct mechanism action.

properties.property: In type 0 servos under steady-state conditions, the system produces a constant value of the output with a constant non-zero error signal.
properties.why: Classification of servos by steady-state feedback control performance.

properties.property: In type 1 servos under steady-state conditions, a constant output produces a null error signal, whereas a constant rate of change of the reference implies a constant error in tracking the reference.
properties.why: Classification of servos by steady-state feedback control performance.

properties.property: In type 2 servos under steady-state conditions, constant output and constant rate of change of reference produce a null error signal, whereas a constant rate of acceleration of reference implies a constant error in tracking.
properties.why: Classification of servos by steady-state feedback control performance.

properties.property: The error signal is defined for measurable physical variables such as position, speed, and attitude.
properties.why: Servomechanisms require feedback signals obtained from transducers (e.g., encoders or potentiometers) measuring physical variables.

assumptions.assumption: The controlled output variable is continuously or periodically measured by an automatic feedback transducer (such as an encoder or potentiometer).
assumptions.breaks_when: There is no automatic feedback mechanism (e.g., open-loop control as in stepper motors, or manual operator observation).

assumptions.assumption: An amplifier or gain mechanism is present to convert and amplify the error signal into corrective actuation.
assumptions.breaks_when: The feedback system lacks an amplifier or gain to drive actuation toward reducing the error (e.g., a windmill fantail).

failure_modes.signature: Discrepancy between actual physical position and sensed feedback, causing an inaccurate error signal and output offset
failure_modes.cause: Temperature changes affecting potentiometer resistance in potentiometer-based feedback sensors

failure_modes.signature: Persistent non-zero error signal under steady-state or dynamic reference tracking
failure_modes.cause: Servo type order is insufficient for the trajectory dynamics (e.g., type 0 with constant output, type 1 tracking a ramp input, or type 2 tracking an accelerating reference)

failure_modes.signature: Large dynamic error signal and inability of the output to follow commanded trajectory
failure_modes.cause: Commanded input changes at a frequency exceeding the servo bandwidth
